  "text": "At seven Tobias went to the church, though it was Thursday and there would be no service. He sat in the last pew with his cap between his knees. The wool smelled of rain. It had not rained.

He waited until the woman who arranged the flowers came through the side door. She asked whether he was ill. He said he had been awake a long time.

From the churchyard he could see Maren's roof. Nothing else. He had chosen that place years ago for the little it allowed him to see.

At nine he took the road to her house.

The eleven posts stood straight beside the path. Her lantern lay on its side between the fourth and fifth. He picked it up by the handle and carried it carefully, keeping the glass clear of his leg.

The door was shut. He knocked once, then tried the latch.

Inside, the lamp stood unlit on the sill. The rug lay flat. There were no wet marks on the boards, no sand. He stayed in the doorway and called her name with the ordinary impatience of someone bringing back a borrowed thing.

When no one answered, he put the lantern down outside.

He would have to tell someone. He tried the words while looking at the latch. She wasn't home. He had found her lantern.

Before leaving, he pulled the door firmly shut.

The latch settled under his thumb. He kept it there a moment longer, waiting to feel it catch.",

  "text": "He told the woman at the church because she was the first person he found. She had finished with the flowers and was washing a jar beneath the outside tap.

How long had Maren been gone?

He said he didn't know.

The woman turned the tap off. Water continued to fall from the mouth of the jar. She asked whether he had looked upstairs.

He hadn't.

By noon there were four of them at the house. Tobias stayed beside the posts while the others went inside. He heard drawers opening, then someone calling from an upper window to ask which direction her bedroom faced.

Toward the water, he said, although the man could see that for himself.

They took the lantern with them. He almost objected. It seemed important that it should remain where he had put it, but he could give no reason that would help.

That evening he went home and hung his cap above the stove. He ate bread standing at the table. When the church bell struck, he counted without deciding to.

There were seven strokes.

He took down his cap. Beneath it, a small dark patch marked the plaster. He touched the patch with two fingers, then smelled them.

There was nothing he could name.

In the morning he fetched a ladder and examined the roof. A slate had slipped near the chimney. He put it back and came down carefully.

For several days afterward he left the ladder against the wall. Whenever someone came along the road, he went outside before they could knock.",

  "text": "The woman brought the lantern back on a Thursday. She had wrapped it in a flour sack, though the glass was sound.

They had no further use for it, she said.

Tobias took it from her at the gate. He waited for her to say something else. Instead she looked at the ladder and asked if he had finished.

He said he had.

After she left, he carried the ladder to the shed. The pale rectangles where its feet had stood remained in the earth. He scuffed one with his boot, then went inside.

There was oil in the lantern. He could not remember whether there had been oil before. The wick had been trimmed neatly, with one corner lower than the other.

He set it on the table and unwrapped the sack. A little flour remained in a seam. He brushed it into his palm and carried it to the door.

That night someone passed along the road without stopping. He heard the footsteps from his chair and stood until they were gone.

In the morning he took the lantern to Maren's house. He had meant to leave it outside again, but rain was gathering on the step, so he tried the door.

It opened.

He put the lantern on the kitchen shelf. Beside it lay a button and a folded piece of paper. He left both untouched.

Before going, he moved the lantern farther back, where it would not fall if someone reached past it.

Then he shut the door, testing the latch twice with his thumb.",
